lead: Grid computing pools computers owned by different organisations into one virtual supercomputer. Each site keeps its own machines and policy; shared standard protocols let a user reach them as one system. The set of users allowed to share is a virtual organisation (VO). A grid is not a cluster, which one owner controls, and not a cloud, which is rented on demand. Grids suit large batch jobs needing many CPU-hours (one CPU busy for one hour). Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.4 for the cloud comparison and Unit 4 for distributed-system design challenges.

blocks.text: A grid is coordinated resource sharing without central control. It covers CPUs, storage, instruments and software. Each provider keeps its own administrative domain, so no single owner holds every machine or every login. The VO groups users and sites that agree to share for one project; middleware maps a VO identity to local accounts. A grid is loosely coupled and heterogeneous.
A cluster is tightly coupled and has one owner. A cloud rents capacity on demand and meters it, as Chapter 6.4 explains. A grid is contributed capacity under local rules.
The unit of work is a job: a program plus input and a resource request. Grids usually run batch jobs.

The grid architecture has five layers. The fabric layer is the machines, storage and networks at each site. The connectivity layer handles authentication and secure transfer. The resource layer enforces each site's policy for its own resources. The collective layer spans sites: brokers, allocation and directories. The application layer holds user jobs.

The connectivity and resource layers form a narrow neck, like an hourglass. Every job crosses that neck, so standard protocols let many applications use many fabrics. A resource broker accepts a job and does matchmaking: it compares CPU count, memory, disk, software and deadline with free capacity, then asks one or more sites. The broker owns no machines.

A data grid moves large files to the site where computation will run. File transfer tools schedule and restart transfers. Security uses X.509 certificates; delegation lets a job act for its user at a remote site for a limited time. National and international research grids exist as examples.

figure.caption: The broker's schedule for the 800 CPU-hour job: for the first 4 hours all three sites run, and site B's 100 CPUs alone give 400 CPU-hours before B leaves. From 4 to 6.67 h the remaining 60 CPUs supply the last 160 CPU-hours, so the job finishes at 6.67 h, inside the 12 h deadline.

spec.aria: A timeline with one lane per grid site: from 0 to 4 hours site A runs 40 CPUs, site B runs 100 CPUs and site C runs 20 CPUs, totalling 640 CPU-hours; site B then stops, and from 4 to 6.67 hours sites A and C run 60 CPUs to finish the last 160 CPU-hours of the 800 CPU-hour job.

examples.question: A grid has three sites. Site A offers 40 free CPUs for 8 hours. Site B offers 100 free CPUs for 4 hours. Site C offers 20 free CPUs for 12 hours. A job needs 800 CPU-hours and must finish within 12 hours. (a) Find total free capacity in CPU-hours. (b) Give a schedule and its finish time.
steps: Run all 160 CPUs for 4 h: 160 × 4 = 640 CPU-hours; B leaves.
A and C give 60 CPUs; phase 2 = 160 ÷ 60 = 2.67 h.
examples.answer: Total free capacity is 960 CPU-hours; the schedule finishes at 6.67 hours.
examples.check:
cap_a = 40 * 8
cap_b = 100 * 4
cap_c = 20 * 12
total = cap_a + cap_b + cap_c
phase1 = 160 * 4
remaining = 800 - phase1
phase2 = remaining / (40 + 20)
finish = 4 + phase2
print(total)
print(round(finish, 2))

traps: Treating a grid as one administrative domain: each site keeps its own policy and accounts.
Calling a cluster a grid: a cluster has one owner, one scheduler and usually one network.
Calling a cloud a grid: a cloud is rented and metered; a grid is contributed under a VO.
Forgetting CPU-hours: 40 CPUs for 8 hours is 320 CPU-hours, not 40 or 8.
Assuming the broker owns capacity: it only requests capacity from site managers.

quiz.a: The users and sites allowed to share in one grid project.
Every job crosses the narrow connectivity and resource layers; many applications and fabrics use standard protocols there.
Grid: many owners, contributed. Cloud: one provider, rented and metered.

quiz.q: A: 30 CPUs for 6 h; B: 20 CPUs for 9 h. Total CPU-hours?
Job 240 CPU-hours, deadline 6 h. A: 10 CPUs for 12 h; B: 20 CPUs for 6 h. Finish time?
quiz.a: First 6 h: 30×6=180. Then 60 CPU-hours on 10 CPUs take 6 h. Finish 12 h; deadline missed.

quiz.q: Why run site B first in the 800 CPU-hour example?
quiz.a: B leaves earliest at 4 h; using its 100 CPUs first captures 400 CPU-hours before loss.

beyond: Not for the exam. Grid ideas survive in cloud batch queues, workflow systems and federated research clouds. Search for 'resource broker', 'matchmaking' and 'X.509 proxy certificate' to go deeper. Volunteer computing uses the same contributed-capacity model at internet scale.
